Thank you, Maria Claudia. Let me push back on one point. Two delays in two months -- is Pittsburgh still the right supplier for the joint venture?
That is a fair question. As far as I know, both delays had the same cause: the carrier changed the route. The goods seem to have been ready on time both times.
Seem to have been? That sounds like you are not sure.
I am sure about the plant; I have the dates. What I cannot rule out is that the carrier does it again. Routes tend to change in the second half of the year.
So you are telling us there could be a third delay.
I would say a third delay is unlikely, but it is possible, and I would rather give you that caveat now than an apology in October.
Then why not move to a second supplier today?
I concede that we need a backup. Having said that, I stand by Pittsburgh for June. Let me price a second supplier and get back to you by the fifteenth.

After a presentation, most people are afraid of the wrong question. They are afraid of the question they cannot answer. In my experience, that one is easy. You say: I do not know, and I will get back to you by Thursday. The dangerous questions are two others. The first is the loaded question, the one that has the answer built into it, like: why did you lose control of the budget? If you answer it as it is, you have accepted that you lost control. So you take the question apart before you answer it: I would not say we lost control; it seems that two costs arrived in the same month. The second dangerous question is the one you can answer, but only in part. Here, people tend to give the whole answer anyway, because silence feels like weakness. It is not. The strongest answer is usually the one with a caveat: this figure is right, as far as I know, but it assumes that the exchange rate stays where it is. That sentence does not make you look unsure. It makes you look like the only person in the room who has read the assumptions.

Twelve years ago, at the end of a very good presentation, a board member asked me whether we could guarantee delivery by December. I had rehearsed the talk for a week, and I had not rehearsed a single question. I said yes. I said it in two seconds, because I wanted the meeting to end the way it had started. December came, and we delivered in February. Nobody remembered the presentation. Everybody remembered the yes. What I should have said was simple: December is likely, but it depends on one supplier, and I will know for sure in three weeks. That answer would have cost me nothing that afternoon, and it would have saved me a very long spring. Since then, I prepare the questions before I prepare the slides. I write down the ten hardest things anyone could ask, and next to each one I write what I know, what I do not know, and the one sentence I am not going to say.

First, you listen to the whole question without interrupting, even if you already know where it is going. Then, if the question is loaded, you take it apart and you push back on the part that is not true. After that, you say what you know for sure, and you hedge the part that is only probable. Next, you add the caveat that the number or the forecast depends on. Finally, if there is a part you cannot answer, you say so, and you commit to a date to get back to them.
